Work mode, salary, and education: what the data says

A client-facing view of the completed analysis, focused on compensation patterns, remote versus hybrid work, and salary differences across education groups. All numerical results below are synchronized with the final Jupyter notebook.

Executive summary

Key takeaways for the client

The analysis highlights three main patterns: Remote respondents have higher observed annual salaries than Hybrid respondents; mean salary is not the same across all three education groups in the North American sample; and compensation is highly right-skewed, so high-end values can noticeably influence averages. These are observational associations; they do not establish that remote work or education causes higher salaries.

Question 1

Exploratory data analysis

Three requested views of job satisfaction, mean salary by job title, and salary versus age, with anomalies called out explicitly.

Data quality and analysis sample: The supplied file has 20,407 rows. Eight additional rows match other records across all 168 columns; they are treated as repeated records, leaving 20,399 rows for analysis. The original CSV is unchanged. Satisfaction averages use 16,950 valid responses, including scores of 0; 3,448 missing scores and the invalid value 60 are omitted. The age–salary figure uses 20,384 observations after excluding five implausible ages and ten missing ages. These variable-specific filters do not remove otherwise usable salary records from Q2 or Q3.

Select a figure to enlarge it; choose “Full size” to inspect its labels.

Figure 1 · Average job satisfaction by job title

Means and valid response counts are shown; 0 is valid on the 0–10 scale, while 60 is excluded.

Average job satisfaction is fairly similar across most job titles, generally clustering around 7–8 out of 10, with support engineers/analysts reporting the lowest average satisfaction, while the retired category’s average of 10 should be treated cautiously because it is based on only one valid response.

Figure 2 · Mean annual salary by job title

Blue circles show means, orange diamonds show medians, and labels give mean salary and salary response count; gray lines connect each mean and median.

Mean annual salaries differ across job titles, with financial analysts/engineers showing the highest mean at about $501.2k but a median of about $87.2k (n = 46), reflecting the strong influence of the $18.4M salary on the mean, while estimates for very small groups such as retired respondents (n = 2) should be interpreted cautiously.

Figure 3 · Annual salary versus age

The salary axis uses a log scale to show the wide range; five implausible ages (1, 3, 9, 126 and 151) plus ten missing ages were excluded.

Annual salary generally increases from younger to middle-aged respondents but shows substantial variation and several extreme high-income outliers, while the much smaller number of older respondents makes the salary pattern at high ages less reliable.

Outlier assessment

Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, 403 Hybrid salaries (5.17%) and 204 Remote salaries (2.94%) were flagged as potential outliers.

The IQR rule flags unusual values, not proven errors. These salaries were retained to compare arithmetic means, while recognizing that their accuracy is unverified and extreme values can strongly affect both the estimated gap and its uncertainty.

Hybrid upper IQR bound$218,689
Remote upper IQR bound$303,525
Observed difference (Hybrid − Remote)-$16,905

Two-sample t-tests

We test equal population mean salaries (H₀: μH = μR) against a difference in either direction (Hₐ: μH ≠ μR), using α = 0.05.

MethodEqual variances assumed?SE ($)tp-valueDecision at α = 0.05
Manual pooled t-testYes6,524.29-2.5911580.009575Reject H₀
Built-in pooled t-testYes6,524.29-2.5911580.009575Reject H₀
Welch t-testNo6,616.99-2.5548600.010634Reject H₀
Bootstrap-based t-testNo6,621.36-2.5531740.010686Reject H₀

What the pooled p-value means: assuming equal population mean salaries and the test assumptions, a t-statistic at least as extreme in either direction as ±2.591 has a probability of about 0.96%. Since p < 0.05, we reject equal population means.

Bootstrap-based t-test: the standard deviation of the 10,000 bootstrap mean differences estimates the standard error ($6,621.36); it is not divided by √10,000. The observed mean difference is divided by this SE, then compared with a t distribution using Welch’s original-data degrees of freedom (13,092.83). This is an approximate t-based inference.

Welch’s method and the separate-group bootstrap allow different population variances and produce closely matching standard errors. All methods use the same survey data, so agreement does not resolve extreme-value accuracy, representativeness, or confounding.

T-test assumptions and robustness

The exact pooled t-test reference distribution assumes independent responses, normally distributed salaries within each population, and equal population variances. The descriptive statistics indicate strong right skewness, so normality of individual salaries is not asserted here. Independence is assumed and cannot be verified from these data alone.

The large groups (7,800 Hybrid and 6,929 Remote respondents) support a normal approximation for the sampling distribution of the mean difference through the Central Limit Theorem, although extreme salaries can affect its accuracy. Welch’s method relaxes equal variance while still relying on independence and an adequate sampling-distribution approximation. The results are interpreted as approximate inference.

Manual pooled calculation details

The pooled test estimates one common population variance. Sample variances use n − 1 in the denominator.

StepCalculation / result
1 · Sample sizesnH = 7,800; nR = 6,929
2 · Sample meansHybrid $101,813.70; Remote $118,719.17
3 · Sample variances (USD²)Hybrid 120,636,810,097.25; Remote 196,217,320,652.59
4 · Pooled variance (USD²)[(nH − 1)sH² + (nR − 1)sR²] / (nH + nR − 2) = 156,192,033,640.90
5 · Pooled standard deviationsp = √(pooled variance) = $395,211.38
6 · Standard errorsp √(1/nH + 1/nR) = $6,524.29
7 · t-statistic(Hybrid mean − Remote mean) / SE = -2.591158
8 · Degrees of freedom and p-valuedf = 14,727; two-sided p = 0.009575

The built-in test with equal_var=True performs the same pooled calculation and gives the same t-statistic and p-value. Welch’s method estimates uncertainty separately for each group.

Bootstrap mean-salary analysis

10,000 replications with replacement, using 7,800 Hybrid and 6,929 Remote observations per replication.

↔ All three figures are included. Click a tab below to view each plot.

Bootstrap centers: Hybrid $101,793.24; Remote $118,716.90. Dashed lines show the original sample means. The Remote sampling distribution is centered higher and is somewhat more dispersed.
The bootstrap mean difference is about −$16,924, very close to the observed −$16,905. Differences are Hybrid minus Remote, so negative values indicate a higher Remote mean; most resampled differences are below zero.
Each bootstrap mean difference is divided by its bootstrap standard error without subtracting the mean. The standardized distribution has mean ≈ −2.556 and SD = 1, close to the observed t-value using the same bootstrap SE (−2.553, shown in orange). The black dashed line at zero means no difference in mean salary. The small discrepancy between the center and observed t-value reflects finite bootstrap resampling. This is the ordinary bootstrap distribution on a t-statistic scale, rather than a null distribution. Scaling preserves its shape and does not make it normal.

95% confidence intervals

Welch t-based CI(−$29,875.73, −$3,935.22)
Bootstrap percentile CI(−$31,272.46, −$4,875.60)

Under the methods’ assumptions, approximately 95% of confidence intervals constructed from repeated samples would contain the true population mean salary difference.

Both intervals are for Hybrid minus Remote and lie entirely below zero, supporting a higher estimated population mean salary for Remote workers under the inference assumptions.

The percentile interval uses the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap differences; it is slightly wider and shifted downward. The Welch interval uses a symmetric t-distribution approximation.

Confidence-interval assumptions

The percentile method does not impose normality on individual salaries or bootstrap differences, and separate-group resampling does not assume equal population variances. Its validity still depends on independent observations and samples that adequately approximate their respective populations. The Welch formula interval allows unequal variances and relies on an adequate t-distribution approximation.

Median comparison

Hybrid median$77,730
Remote median$90,614
Mood's χ² / p109.0156 / 1.610 × 10⁻²⁵
Bootstrap median p0.000100
Median difference (Hybrid − Remote)−$12,884

Both tests reject equal population medians at α = 0.05. Their p-values are not numerically close: Mood’s test uses counts around the grand median, while the bootstrap test uses the median difference. Both support a higher median salary for Remote respondents.

How the median tests were calculated

Mood’s test classifies salaries above versus at or below the grand median of $81,912 and applies a chi-square test. The separate-group bootstrap uses 10,000 resamples at the original group sizes; its median-difference SE is $1,610.30.

Mood’s median test does not require normally distributed salaries or equal salary variances. It assumes independent observations and sufficiently large expected cell counts for the chi-square approximation. The smallest expected count is approximately 3,464, above the usual guideline of 5.

Salary relative to grand medianHybridRemote
Above $81,9123,5833,781
At or below $81,9124,2173,148

For an approximate null-centered bootstrap test, the observed median difference is subtracted from each bootstrap difference. Absolute null-centered differences are compared with the absolute observed difference. None of the 10,000 replications is as extreme, so the +1 correction gives p = 1/10,001 ≈ 0.000100. This finite simulation cannot resolve a p-value as small as Mood’s analytical result.

ANOVA results

We test equal population mean salaries across all three degrees (H₀: μB = μM = μP) against at least one difference, using α = 0.05.

Standard one-way ANOVAF = 17.4966 · p = 2.70 × 10⁻⁸
Welch ANOVAF = 12.2065 · p = 6.16 × 10⁻⁶
Bootstrap ANOVAp = 0.000100

All three approaches reject equal population means at α = 0.05. ANOVA alone does not identify which specific pairs differ.

ANOVA assumptions and robustness

The standard one-way ANOVA assumes independent observations, normal responses within groups, and equal population variances. Independence is assumed rather than verified. The relatively large group sizes can reduce sensitivity to departures from normality, although strong skewness and extreme salaries can still affect the accuracy of the inference. Unequal sample sizes and noticeably different salary SDs motivate Welch’s ANOVA as a separate check that allows unequal variances.

Bootstrap distributions of mean salary

10,000 replications with replacement, using the original group sizes: Bachelor's 2,978, Master's 1,084, and Professional 301.

↔ All three figures are included. Click a tab below to view each plot.

Bootstrap mean centers: Bachelor's $161,024.86; Master's $182,202.36; Professional $197,530.32. The colored dashed lines show the corresponding original sample means. The Professional distribution is widest, consistent with its smaller sample and larger sample SD, both of which increase uncertainty in the estimated mean.
Colored dashed lines mark the pairwise bootstrap means: Bachelor's−Master's ≈ −$21,178; Bachelor's−Professional ≈ −$36,505; Master's−Professional ≈ −$15,328. These centers are close to the differences between the original sample means. The black dashed line marks no mean salary difference. Both Bachelor's comparisons remain below zero across all 10,000 replications. Comparisons involving the smaller, more variable Professional group have greater uncertainty; Master's−Professional crosses zero. Overall equality of the three population means is assessed by the ANOVA tests.
Each pairwise bootstrap difference is divided by its own bootstrap standard error without subtracting its mean, so each standardized distribution has SD = 1. Colored dashed lines mark the means: Bachelor's−Master's ≈ −3.970; Bachelor's−Professional ≈ −3.183; Master's−Professional ≈ −1.233. These nearly coincide with the corresponding observed t-values using the same bootstrap SEs (−3.980, −3.201, and −1.245); the small discrepancies reflect finite bootstrap resampling. The black dashed line marks no mean salary difference, and Master's−Professional crosses it. These are descriptive pairwise bootstrap distributions, rather than null distributions or formal pairwise significance tests. Distribution overlap alone does not establish whether population means differ significantly. Scaling preserves shape and does not make the distributions normal.
Bootstrap ANOVA: the observed F-statistic is 17.4966. In 10,000 null bootstrap replications, none produced an F-statistic at least this large. With the finite-bootstrap +1 correction, p ≈ 0.0001, agreeing with the original ANOVA conclusion. Each group’s mean is subtracted from its salaries, the resulting residuals are pooled, and null samples are drawn from that pool at the original group sizes with the common grand mean added back. This imposes a common mean and residual shape and variance. The bootstrap p-value uses the empirical null distribution of the F-statistic rather than assuming normally distributed raw salaries. Welch’s ANOVA separately checks sensitivity to unequal variances. The original ANOVA uses a theoretical F distribution, while the bootstrap uses finite resampling; with no extreme replications, its smallest corrected p-value is 1/10,001 ≈ 0.000100.
Methodology & interpretation

How to read the results

Plain-language explanations of the statistical tools used in the notebook.

What does a p-value mean here?

A p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true and the method’s assumptions hold, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true.

What does bootstrapping do?

Bootstrapping repeatedly resamples the observed data with replacement to approximate the sampling distribution of a statistic. The analysis uses 10,000 replications and the original group sample sizes.

Why keep potential salary outliers?

Compensation is strongly right-skewed, and very high salaries can be legitimate. IQR rules flag statistical extremes, not necessarily errors. Without direct evidence of data-entry problems, the analysis retains these observations.

Why use Welch tests as robustness checks?

Observed group standard deviations differ, and group sizes are unequal. Welch procedures allow unequal population variances. Agreement shows that the decision is consistent under the variance treatments examined; all methods still rely on the same survey data and their inference assumptions.

Inference and business interpretation

Responses are treated as independent, but this cannot be confirmed from the data alone. Large samples support approximate inference for means, while strong skewness and extreme values can still affect its accuracy. Population interpretations depend on survey representativeness. Experience, job role and location are not controlled here, so these associations support further investigation rather than establishing causal effects of work mode or education.
